title: Why do People Struggle to Stick to Their Financial Resolutions?
summary: Money resolutions break at five plain points. See how to turn one into an amount, a date and an automatic monthly step, with a worked example.
body_markdown:
People struggle to keep financial resolutions when they are vague, too big a change at once and left to willpower. The first emergency or busy month then ends them. Resolutions last longer when they have an amount, a date and a monthly step that runs on its own. This article covers where resolutions break and how to build one that bends instead.


## Why do people struggle to stick to their financial resolutions?


A money resolution can break at one of five points: it is vague, it is too big a jump, it depends on willpower, nobody checks it, or an emergency lands early.


**It is vague.** "Save more this year" has no finish line. In March you cannot tell whether you succeeded, so nothing pulls you back on a bad month.


**It is too big a jump.** Going from saving nothing to saving a large part of your pay is a new lifestyle overnight. The first month feels like punishment, and the second month is skipped.


**It depends on willpower.** If you must decide to save every month, you are making the decision at the very moment the money is in your account and the bills, sales and invitations are all asking for it.


**Nobody checks it.** Without a look at the numbers once a month, a small slip goes unnoticed until it has become the habit.


**The first emergency ends it.** A medical bill or a repair in month two takes the savings you just built. With no plan for that, the resolution feels dead.


Money also behaves differently depending on its label. This habit is called mental accounting: treating money differently depending on where it came from or which "pot" it sits in. A bonus feels like free money, so it is spent, even though the resolution said to save. The[common behavioural biases](https://koshex.com/blog/common-behavioural-biases-investors-must-avoid) article covers more of these habits of the mind.


## How do you turn a resolution into a plan?


Give the resolution a rupee amount, a date and a monthly step, and write down where the money will sit.


Take Meera, an example person. Her monthly expenses are ₹42,000, which is an assumed figure for this illustration. She decides on three months of expenses as her emergency target. An emergency fund is money kept aside for sudden costs such as a job loss or a hospital bill, and[Where to keep your emergency savings](https://koshex.com/blog/where-should-you-keep-your-emergency-savings) puts it at three to six months of expenses.


Her vague resolution, "save more this year", becomes this:


- Amount: ₹1,26,000, which is three months of ₹42,000.
- Date: 31 March.
- Monthly step: starting 1 April, ₹10,500 a month for 12 months (₹1,26,000 ÷ 12).
- Where it sits: a separate account, not the one her salary lands in.


Now March has a finish line, and every month has a number to hit. For a plan of this kind, a budget helps: a plan for what you will spend and what you will keep aside each month. The[guide to money management](https://koshex.com/blog/the-ultimate-guide-to-money-management) shows how to build one. The[50-30-20 rule](https://koshex.com/blog/50-30-20-rule) is a rule of thumb some people use to split income, not a regulation. For the full goal-setting method, see[financial planning for beginners](https://koshex.com/blog/the-ultimate-guide-to-financial-planning-for-beginners) .


### What other resolutions do people make?


These are common examples, shown as illustrations and not as things anyone must do.


- **Start or raise a SIP.** A SIP is investing a fixed amount at regular intervals, usually monthly. Try the[SIP calculator](https://koshex.com/calculators/sip-calculator) to see how an instalment adds up over time.
- **Clear the most expensive debt.** The[debt trap guide](https://koshex.com/blog/5-steps-to-get-out-of-a-debt-trap) explains how debt builds up and how to get out of it.
- **Settle your tax regime early.** The old tax regime is the older set of income-tax rules, which allows deductions such as section 123 (the old Section 80C). The new tax regime is the default, with lower rates and few deductions. The new regime applies unless you opt out. If you have no business income, you choose the old regime in your return each year, so file it by the due date. Telling your employer only decides how much tax is deducted from your salary; your return decides your tax.
- **Spread section 123 investments across the year.** Section 123 (the old Section 80C) counts deductions only up to ₹1,50,000 in a tax year, in the old regime only. The[tax-saving guide](https://koshex.com/blog/how-to-save-tax-in-india-tax-saving-guide) has the details, and[money tasks for the start of the financial year](https://koshex.com/blog/things-to-do-at-the-start-of-the-financial-year) lists what to check each April.
- **Name nominees on every account.** A nominee is the person you name to receive the money if you die. The[mutual fund nomination](https://koshex.com/blog/mutual-fund-nomination) article shows how it works for funds.


## How do you make the plan run without willpower?


Automate it, so the money moves on payday before you can spend it.


For an investment, that means a SIP with a one-time mandate: a one-time mandate lets the fund house collect each SIP instalment from your bank account automatically. The[one-time mandate article](https://koshex.com/blog/one-time-mandate-otm-sip) explains the mechanics.


For the emergency pot, the same idea applies. Set up a standing instruction to your bank to move a fixed sum on payday from your salary account to the separate account. Money that never reaches the spending account cannot be spent on a whim.


When your pay rises, raise the amount too. This is called a step-up: raising the SIP when income rises is one way to invest more over time. Here is the arithmetic only, with no return assumed. A ₹5,000 SIP raised by ₹500 after an April pay rise means ₹66,000 paid in over the next 12 months instead of ₹60,000. The[step-up SIP](https://koshex.com/blog/step-up-sip) article has more. A step-up amount is your own choice, not a recommended rate.


## How do you track progress without giving up?


Check once a month against the plan's own numbers, not against how you feel.


A short monthly routine is enough:


1. Compare the balance in the separate account with the target for that month. For Meera, after three months the target is ₹31,500.
2. Look at where the rest of the money went. The[guide to tracking your expenses](https://koshex.com/blog/track-your-personal-expenses) shows simple ways to do it.
3. Note one thing to change next month, if anything.


Once or twice a year, work out your net worth, which is what you own minus what you owe. The[four pillars of personal finance](https://koshex.com/blog/the-four-pillars-of-personal-finance) article explains how. Seeing it rise, even slowly, is a more honest sign of progress than a good month.


Telling a partner or a friend your target also helps, because it gives the resolution a witness. If you want help,[questions to ask a financial advisor](https://koshex.com/blog/5-important-questions-to-ask-your-financial-advisor) lists what to check before hiring one.


## What should you do when you slip?


Recalculate instead of restarting.


Say Meera misses the first month, April. The remaining 11 months now need about ₹11,455 each (₹1,26,000 ÷ 11). Or she moves the date one month later and keeps ₹10,500. Either way, the plan survives. A slip is a recalculation, not a failure.


If an emergency used the money, rebuild that pot first, and let the other resolutions wait.


Market falls test a different kind of resolution. SEBI's investor website says: "A smart investor will not panic and sell their investments when the market takes a downturn. Instead, they will stay calm and focus on their long-term goals." SEBI is the Securities and Exchange Board of India, the market regulator. If your money is under strain, you can pause or stop a SIP, and[how to stop or pause a SIP](https://koshex.com/blog/how-to-stop-or-pause-a-sip) covers how.


A resolution that bends is still working. One that breaks silently is the one to worry about.
